item.title: ‘Money wasted’: Chief Justice criticises COI legal advice
item.description: CHIEF Justice Salesi Temo has criticised the legal advice given to President Ratu Naiqama Lalabalavu over the extension of the Commission of Inquiry into the appointment of former FICAC commissioner Barbara Malimali, saying lawyers had failed to properly examine the limits of the President’s powers. item.content:encoded:
CHIEF Justice Salesi Temo has criticised the legal advice given to President Ratu Naiqama Lalabalavu over the extension of the Commission of Inquiry into the appointment of former FICAC commissioner Barbara Malimali, saying lawyers had failed to properly examine the limits of the President’s powers.

Justice Temo made the comments while addressing newly admitted lawyers, using the inquiry as an example of the importance of providing accurate legal advice and understanding the limits imposed by legislation.

He described the outcome as “money wasted”, saying the responsibility lay with the lawyers rather than the clients who relied on their advice.

“We’ve got to work and find out what are the parameters of your power to continue with that legal work,” Justice Temo said.

He referred to the High Court judgment of Justice Dane Tuiqereqere, which found that the President did not have the power under the Commission of Inquiry Act to extend the inquiry beyond the statutory period.

“Lawyers were hired from overseas and they didn’t read the COI Act properly to show that His Excellency the President doesn’t have the power to extend it.

“As a result, all the work that they did later was pronounced ultra vires and null and void.”

The Chief Justice said the failure to identify the legal limitation resulted in the commission continuing its hearings without valid legal authority, adding that the matter demonstrated the responsibility lawyers had to examine legislation carefully and determine the limits of their clients’ legal powers.

“That is your work as lawyers, to dig, dig, dig. Obviously, the lawyer involved in that (advising the President) was amiss, (and) didn’t find it.

When approached by The Fiji Times separately about the same High Court judgment that raised concerns of the appropriateness of Ms Malimali’s appointment, the Chief Justice declined to comment and directed questions to Justice Dane Tuiqereqere who delivered the judgment.

Justice Temo is the chairman of the Judicial Service Commission, which handled key judicial appointments, including the position of FiCAC Commissioner.

While ruling the findings of the COI null and void after finding the inquiry was tainted by bias and breached the rules of natural justice, Justice Tuiqereqere said it had served its purpose. He said Ms Malimali was not appropriate for the post in light of an active criminal investigation and an incident in Tuvalu.

item.title: Fire destroys Drasa grower’s farm
item.description: DRASA sector grower Nilesh Prasad lost 90 per cent of his farm to an uncontrollable fire that claimed close to 100 tonnes of sugar cane and $3000 worth of pineapple. Mr Prasad said their attempts to put out the fire last Wednesday was futile because of the dry conditions.
item.content:encoded:
DRASA sector grower Nilesh Prasad lost 90 per cent of his farm to an uncontrollable fire that claimed close to 100 tonnes of sugar cane and $3000 worth of pineapple.

Mr Prasad said their attempts to put out the fire last Wednesday was futile because of the dry conditions.

“We don’t usually get this kind of fire that spread so quickly,” said Mr Prasad. “It started from one very small end of the cane field, and it quickly spread to the other sections.

“The fire started around 3pm and it took about three hours for us to control it.” He said the dry conditions had made it worse.

“It’s been very dry. So when a fire starts, it spreads very quickly.”

Mr Prasad’s farm and many others located within the Western Division had fallen victim to indiscriminate burning. Sugar Cane Growers Council CEO Vimal Dutt said stakeholders had been briefed about the prolonged dry spell they anticipate would also impact the sugar industry.

“We are expecting issues of farms burning, water supply going low and food security concerns,” he said.

“So we are doing our best to implement some immediate and long term measures for our growers.”

Nilesh Prasad (middle) with his labourers at his farm in Drasa, Lautoka. Picture: REINAL CHAND

item.title: Grey listing risk
item.description: FIJI could face serious economic consequences, including possible grey listing, if it fails an international assessment of its anti-money laundering and financial crime measures next month. Justice Minister Siromi Turaga told Parliament Fiji’s money laundering risk remained high, with drug offences, organised crime, tax and customs crimes, illegal fishing, bribery and corruption identified among t
item.content:encoded:
FIJI could face serious economic consequences, including possible grey listing, if it fails an international assessment of its anti-money laundering and financial crime measures next month.

Justice Minister Siromi Turaga told Parliament Fiji’s money laundering risk remained high, with drug offences, organised crime, tax and customs crimes, illegal fishing, bribery and corruption identified among the key threats.

“It is important that Fiji does well in the mutual evaluation,” Mr Turaga said.

He warned that an unfavourable outcome could result in grey listing by international partners and financial institutions.

The Asia Pacific Group on money laundering assessment will examine Fiji’s legal framework as well as how effectively authorities investigate and prosecute financial crimes, use financial intelligence and confiscate criminal assets.

An assessment team is expected in Fiji in September for discussions and interviews with Government and private sector representatives.

Mr Turaga said Fiji had made significant progress since its previous assessment in 2015, including the establishment of a dedicated civil forfeiture unit within the Office of the Director of Public Prosecutions.

He said forfeiture cases had increased, with the biggest recent case involving almost $9million in properties.

Active cases currently involve about $11m in assets, most linked to drug-related cases.

Mr Turaga said the assessment outcome would influence decisions by institutions including the IMF, World Bank and international banks on investment, financing and trade with Fiji.

item.title: AOG Fiji breaks ground for new HQ
item.description: The Assemblies of God of Fiji has begun construction of a new $17.9million seven-storey headquarters in Suva, with church leaders describing the project as the fulfilment of a vision developed over several years. Reverend Filikesa Koroivueta said the project was driven by the church’s general superintendent Reverend Moses Cakau, who took up the vision with “zeal and passion” about two to three yea
item.content:encoded:
The Assemblies of God of Fiji has begun construction of a new $17.9million seven-storey headquarters in Suva, with church leaders describing the project as the fulfilment of a vision developed over several years.

Reverend Filikesa Koroivueta said the project was driven by the church’s general superintendent Reverend Moses Cakau, who took up the vision with “zeal and passion” about two to three years ago.

He said the building would become a landmark in Suva and provide members with a sense of pride and belonging. The project was first developed in 2021 with construction expected to take 15 months and will use prefabricated materials.

The church also plans to develop its Bible School on iTaukei land and utilise vacant land in Koronivia provided by the Ministry of Lands, with part of the property earmarked for commercial development to support its ministries and schools.

item.title: Rabuka rejects court’s finding
item.description: PRIME Minister Sitiveni Rabuka has rejected the High Court finding that he and the President had a duty to give those affected by the Commission of Inquiry, an opportunity to respond before the report was made public. The finding, made by High Court Judge Justice Dane Tuiqereqere, is among the specific grounds Mr Rabuka is challenging in his appeal, according to his legal representative Simione Va
item.content:encoded:
PRIME Minister Sitiveni Rabuka has rejected the High Court finding that he and the President had a duty to give those affected by the Commission of Inquiry, an opportunity to respond before the report was made public.

The finding, made by High Court Judge Justice Dane Tuiqereqere, is among the specific grounds Mr Rabuka is challenging in his appeal, according to his legal representative Simione Valenitabua.

Mr Valenitabua said the Prime Minister disagreed with the court’s conclusion that, because the Commissioner Justice David Ashton-Lewis had failed to give notice of draft adverse findings, the responsibility fell on the Prime Minister and the President to give the affected parties an opportunity to respond before the report was released publicly.

In a statement, Mr Valenitabua said the legal team considered the finding a “fundamental error of law”.

“The appeal would specifically challenge the findings in paragraphs 372 and 374 of the judgment,” Mr Valenitabua said.

He said the Prime Minister’s legal team argues that there was no legal duty on the Prime Minister or the President to issue to individuals specific letters or notices or equivalent opportunities to respond to findings of an advisory report before its publication.

He said the Prime Minister’s lawyers maintained that the procedural obligations of an independent inquiry, including the requirement to afford natural justice, rested with the commissioner conducting the inquiry.

“Our client and His Excellency the President of Fiji cannot, and should not, act as appellate reviewers of an independent commission’s internal procedures.”

The legal team also argues that the executive had a constitutional duty to transparently release commissioned reports of high national interest to the public.

“We will seek to separate his lawful executive actions from the procedural missteps of the independent commission.

“The executive is not legally responsible for curing the procedural defects of an independent commission prior to publication.”

The appeal is expected to be filed and served after the High Court determines costs and damages.

Mr Valenitabua also said the Prime Minister’s successful defence of the COI’s establishment was personally funded and that the appeal would likewise be the same.

item.title: Bank aligns energy
item.description: Investment Fiji has commended financial institution BRED Bank (Fiji) Pte Limited for its sponsorship of the Excellence in Innovation Award at the upcoming Prime Minister’s International Business Awards (PMIBA) 2026. Marking its first year as a PMIBA sponsor, the French-owned bank is supporting a national award that has recognised Fijian business achievements for more than three decades.
item.content:encoded:
Investment Fiji has commended financial institution BRED Bank (Fiji) Pte Limited for its sponsorship of the Excellence in Innovation Award at the upcoming Prime Minister’s International Business Awards (PMIBA) 2026.

Marking its first year as a PMIBA sponsor, the French-owned bank is supporting a national award that has recognised Fijian business achievements for more than three decades.

BRED Bank (Fiji) chief executive officer Pierre Tastet said BRED Bank was proud to partner with Investment Fiji “because this award strongly aligns with the bank’s commitment to supporting businesses that are driving economic transformation through new ideas, improved processes and sustainable value creation”.

“Through this sponsorship, BRED Bank is pleased to align its energies with Investment Fiji and the wider business community to support initiatives that create opportunities, encourage investment and promote responsible business growth,” Mr Tastet said.

Investment Fiji chief executive officer Kamal Chetty said the bank’s support was well matched with the 2026 theme – ‘Economic Transformation and Inclusive Growth’.

He said the theme focused on businesses that were helping Fiji move into higher-value industries, use digital tools more effectively and create opportunities beyond the main urban centres.

“We are delighted to welcome BRED Bank to the Prime Minister’s International Business Awards partnership. Its support will help us highlight businesses that are responding to challenges with innovation and clear results,” Mr Chetty said in statement.

“These are the businesses that can open new markets, create jobs and contribute to a stronger and more inclusive economy.

“We look forward to building this relationship in the years ahead,” Mr Chetty said.

The Excellence in Innovation Award celebrates businesses that turn new ideas into practical results.

It is designed for organisations that have introduced new or improved products, services, processes or business strategies that help them work more efficiently, serve customers better or grow in a sustainable way.

Applications for PMIBA 2026 are open, and entrants will need to show what changed, why it mattered and how innovation improved productivity or created value for the business and its customers.

item.title: Valenitabua: COI concerns were valid
item.description: JUDICIAL findings that concerns over Barbara Malimali’s suitability for the position of FICAC Commissioner were valid “completely dismantle” claims that the Commission of Inquiry (COI) was a baseless political exercise, Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka’s lawyer Simione Valenitabua says. In a statement, Mr Valenitabua said the High Court’s decision to quash the COI report on procedural and technical
item.content:encoded:
JUDICIAL findings that concerns over Barbara Malimali’s suitability for the position of FICAC Commissioner were valid “completely dismantle” claims that the Commission of Inquiry (COI) was a baseless political exercise, Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka’s lawyer Simione Valenitabua says.

In a statement, Mr Valenitabua said the High Court’s decision to quash the COI report on procedural and technical grounds did not invalidate the concerns that prompted the inquiry into Ms Malimali’s appointment. He rejected claims that the judgment amounted to a complete vindication for Ms Malimali or that the COI was a waste of public funds.

“While the High Court quashed the COI Report on procedural and technical grounds (which we disagree with), the court explicitly validated the foundational concerns of the executive that led to the establishment of the independent COI,” Mr Valenitabua said.

He drew attention to paragraphs 365 and 366 of the judgment, saying the High Court recognised the significance of the active criminal investigation and undisclosed international disciplinary issues in assessing Ms Malimali’s suitability for Fiji’s highest anti-corruption office.

At paragraph 365, the court stated that FICAC’s work was vital to Fiji’s economic and social integrity and that the appointment of its commissioner was critical to its success.

It found that, “for this reason alone”, the establishment of the COI into Ms Malimali’s appointment in October 2024 “served a useful purpose”.

At paragraph 366, the court found that the COI report had raised valid concerns about the appointment process, including the relevance of the “Tuvalu incident” and an active FICAC criminal investigation to Ms Malimali’s suitability.

The court further stated that these matters should have been disclosed to the Judicial Service Commission and that it was not appropriate for Ms Malimali to be appointed while an active criminal investigation against her remained pending.

Mr Valenitabua said the findings demonstrated that the concerns behind the inquiry were legitimate.

“These judicial findings completely dismantle any assertion that the COI was a baseless political exercise.”

item.title: Overcrowding takes toll
item.description: TEACHERS are seeking medication from St Giles Psychiatric Hospital because of stress, pressure and sickness, Fijian Teachers Association (FTA) general secretary Paula Manumanunitoga reveals. Speaking in an interview yesterday about the high absenteeism rate among teachers, Mr Manumanunitoga said the large number of students in classrooms was a major contributing factor to the “enormous levels of s
item.content:encoded:
TEACHERS are seeking medication from St Giles Psychiatric Hospital because of stress, pressure and sickness, Fijian Teachers Association (FTA) general secretary Paula Manumanunitoga reveals.

Speaking in an interview yesterday about the high absenteeism rate among teachers, Mr Manumanunitoga said the large number of students in classrooms was a major contributing factor to the “enormous levels of stress” teachers face.

He pointed to schools in the Suva area where student numbers can reach 55 in a classroom.

“Now, how do we expect a teacher to be mindful of his absence because of the stress levels that he has to bear with for 14 whole weeks during a term before he actually gets a break,” he said.

Mr Manumanunitoga said weekends were sometimes not enough for teachers to recover from the demands of dealing with large numbers of students throughout the week.

“Teachers have to manage their stress levels, they would want to have a rest because of the large class sizes that they have, the population that they have.”

He said the FTA had previously been raising the issue of overcrowded classrooms with the ministry and had made suggestions, including encouraging faith-based schools to construct more classrooms or expand existing ones.

Mr Manumanunitoga said teachers should not be compared with other civil servants because of the demands of their work.

He said teachers were required to be “yapping away from 7 in the mornings until 3 in the afternoons” to carry out their duties.

“They are doing the job of disseminating knowledge, whereas other civil servants sit in front of a computer in the office.”

He said the stress levels between teachers and other civil servants were different, despite being categorised under the same system.

Mr Manumanunitoga said a job evaluation was needed to determine whether the current classification properly reflected the demands placed on teachers.
